title: MEP-CMAP Analyser

creators.name: Andrushko, Justin W.
creators.affiliation: School of Sport, Exercise and Rehabilitation, Northumbria University, Newcastle upon Tyne, UK

description:
MEP-CMAP Analyser is a BIDS-compliant, open-source, cross-platform desktop application for processing, quantifying and group-analysing transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and electromyography (EMG) neurophysiology recordings. It is built for researchers who need reproducible, auditable waveform analysis without writing custom scripts for every study.

The tool is not limited to a single measure or paradigm. It handles motor evoked potentials (MEPs), compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs), cortical silent periods (cSPs), M-wave recruitment curves, paired-pulse protocols such as short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI) and intracortical facilitation (ICF), and any other time-locked EMG response measurable by peak-to-peak amplitude, onset latency or area under the curve. It operates on continuous recordings, pre-epoched trial stacks, and EMG bursts recorded without stimulation.

Capabilities

  • Direct import of Spike2, LabChart, EDF/BDF, AcqKnowledge and generic delimited text files, with a guided one-time wizard for arbitrary tabular layouts
  • Configurable filtering, including band-pass, notch and harmonic suppression, with live preview
  • Automated detection of response onset, peak-to-peak amplitude, root-mean-square amplitude, area under the curve and cortical silent period duration, each overridable per trial
  • Automated outlier screening with an interactive review step, so exclusion decisions are explicit, persistent and recorded in the output
  • An interactive per-trial data inspector for marker adjustment, annotation and exclusion
  • Mmax normalisation with robust plateau detection across full recruitment curves, supramaximal clusters or a single M-wave
  • Compensation of evoked-potential magnitude for pre-stimulus spinal motoneurone excitability by quantile regression, following the method of Carson (2026, Journal of Physiology 604.14, 5731-5757), verified against the author's published reference implementation
  • Paired-pulse ratio computation with multiple reference assignments per file
  • Trial-level and summary CSV output, a group-level file formatted for linear mixed-effects modelling, per-trial waveform bundles, and BIDS-style derivatives with provenance

Changes in version 1.3.2

  • Correction: trial-level columns were shifted by one place. Per-trial rows are assembled as positional lists, and the code filling the z-score and detrended fields addressed them by literal index. Those literals were each one lower than the column they named, so Z_PTP_Pooled received the within-condition detrended amplitude in millivolts, PTP_Detrended_WithinCond(mV) received a z-score, PTP_Detrended_WithinCond_Z received the session-detrended amplitude, PTP_Detrended_Session(mV) received a z-score, PTP_Detrended_Session_Z was never written at all, and Z_PreStimRMS was overwritten with the within-condition amplitude z-score. The fault is visible in an affected file as columns labelled (mV) holding values on a z-score scale and the reverse. Every such write now resolves its position from the column definition by name, so the row layout and the code writing into it cannot disagree again.
  • Correction: two definitions of pre-stimulus RMS. The shared quantification module is documented as the single source of truth for scalar trial metrics, but nothing called it, and its pre-stimulus RMS did not remove the direct-current offset while the analysis pipeline did. The two differed by approximately ten percent on a segment carrying a modest offset, so an add-on following the documented interface obtained a value that silently contradicted the PreStimRMS column. The shared function now removes the offset by default and the pipeline delegates to it, so one implementation serves both. Per-trial peak-to-peak amplitude, RMS and area under the curve are now computed through these shared functions as well. Trial values are unchanged by this item; only the standalone helper moved, onto the correct value.
  • New measure: MEP RMS. Root-mean-square amplitude over the same window as peak-to-peak, reported per trial as MEP_RMS(mV) with matching summary and averaged-waveform columns. Peak-to-peak amplitude is determined by two extreme samples and is therefore sensitive to a single spike, whereas RMS integrates the whole response, so a broad low-amplitude response and a narrow spiky one of equal peak-to-peak amplitude are no longer indistinguishable.
  • New pre-epoched MATLAB reader. Trial stacks already cut around the stimulus are read directly, with the analysis windows clamped to the extent the file actually contains and a warning when the available post-stimulus window is too short for cortical silent period detection.
  • New variability add-on (first level). Trial-to-trial variability per stimulus type: the coefficient of variation in raw, small-sample corrected, logarithmic and robust forms with confidence intervals; median absolute deviation and interquartile range, each scaled so that all three estimate the same quantity under normality; robust and logarithmic z scores; the precision of a condition mean and the number of trials required to tighten it; autoregressive structure and within-session drift; limits of agreement between independent trials and between k-trial averages; the typical error of measurement and the associated root mean square error family; contrasts between conditions; and correlations among trial-level measures. Every dispersion metric is also reported with and without robust-z outliers, and a leave-one-out jackknife shows how far each single trial moves the estimate.
  • New variability_group add-on (second level). Dataset-level reliability from the merged group table: variance decomposed into between-participant, between-session and trial-level components; the reliability, standard error of measurement and minimal detectable change of a measurement averaged over any number of trials and sessions; the intraclass correlation in its one-way random, absolute agreement and consistency forms with their k-measurement variants; and session-to-session agreement. Results may be split by between-participant design factors read from the study design.
  • Whether variability should be analysed on the raw or logarithmic scale is measured rather than assumed. The group add-on regresses the logarithm of the standard deviation on the logarithm of the mean across recordings. A slope near zero indicates additive noise, for which the standard deviation is the meaningful summary; a slope near one indicates noise proportional to amplitude, for which the coefficient of variation is appropriate and the logarithmic scale is the natural one. The verdict is taken from the confidence interval, and reports honestly when a dataset cannot distinguish the two. The add-on also reports whether the choice of dispersion metric changes which recordings rank as most variable.
  • Reliability is distinguished from change. Design factors are classified by whether they vary within a participant. Between-participant factors may be split on, so between-session reliability survives within each stratum; within-participant factors such as timepoint label the repeated-measures axis instead, because splitting on one would leave a single session per participant. A session pair straddling an intervention is reported as measuring change rather than test-retest reliability, since its limits of agreement reflect measurement error together with whatever genuinely changed.
  • Figures are now accompanied by a plain-language caption file containing that recording's own values, explaining each panel and flagging interpretation hazards only when the data raises them, such as a drift that inflates the coefficient of variation, or a typical error inflated by trial-to-trial alternation.
  • Add-on settings may now declare a fixed list of options, or a list read from the columns the open dataset actually contains, rendering as a dropdown rather than a text field. Boolean settings render as a checkbox.
  • An installation of MNE-Python whose readers cannot load, most often a version mismatch against SciPy, is now treated as unavailable rather than being offered and failing later when a file is opened.

Note on reproducibility: existing derivatives should be reprocessed. The column-alignment correction described above changes the contents of six columns in every trial-level file written by earlier versions, and populates a seventh that was always empty. Any analysis that used the detrended amplitudes, the pooled amplitude z-score or the standardised pre-stimulus RMS should be repeated after reprocessing. Peak-to-peak amplitude, onset latency, area under the curve, the cortical silent period measures, the excitability-compensated amplitudes and the stored waveforms were not affected, so any analysis resting only on those is unchanged. Datasets analysed with the excitability compensation in version 1.2.5 or earlier should also still be reprocessed, as noted for version 1.2.8.
